overview: This 94-page file brings together 58 State Department, diplomatic, military, naval, and consular documents from 1938–1939 concerning suspected Japanese activities in Mexico. Reports, memoranda, despatches, press clippings, translations, and cross-reference notes track Japanese fishing fleets and immigration, alleged espionage and coastal reconnaissance, commercial propaganda, and efforts to secure petroleum, salt, mineral, construction, and infrastructure interests. Concentrated especially on Baja California, the Gulf of California, Sonora, Guerrero, Michoacán, Veracruz, and the Poza Rica oil region, the file documents both genuine Japanese economic engagement and the expanding U.S. security apparatus monitoring it. Many claims rested on rumors, private informants, overheard conversations, or contemporary anti-Japanese assumptions and therefore require careful corroboration.
interest: Shows how commercial ventures in Mexico became entangled with espionage fears, and how contradictory intelligence circulated.
